title: Memory, I/O interfacing and interrupts
subtitle: Connecting real chips to the bus so the processor reaches each one at exactly the right address.

sections.title: Address decoding
sections.body:
Imagine a street where every house must answer only its own number. If two houses answered at once, you would hear nonsense. A processor’s bus is that street. Each memory or I/O chip has a chip-select input; address decoding turns the high address lines into select signals so exactly one chip responds. Full (unique) decoding uses all the high lines, so each location has one address. Partial (non-unique) decoding ignores some, so the chip appears at several addresses, with simpler hardware. Decoders (74LS138 3-to-8) or NAND gates generate the selects.

Work one out. An 8 KB RAM (2000H–3FFFH) on an 8085: 8 KB = 2¹³, so A0–A12 go to the chip. The range 2000H–3FFFH has A15A14A13 = 001, so those three lines drive the decoder. Why must decoding ensure only one chip responds? Otherwise two chips would drive the bus at once and corrupt the data.

worked.why: An 8 KB RAM (2000H–3FFFH) on an 8085. Which lines select it?
8 KB = 2¹³, so A0–A12 go to the chip. The range 2000H–3FFFH has A15A14A13 = 001.

questions.prompt: Why must address decoding ensure only one chip responds?

choices.text: Two chips driving the data bus at once would cause bus contention and corrupt data.

figures.caption: Figure 4.1.1 — a decoder selects a chip
figures.note: Three upper address lines pick one 8 KB block.
figures.script:
diagram("direction: right
[A15 A14 A13] as hi #blue
[3-to-8 decoder] as dec #violet
[Y0 → ROM 0000-1FFF] as y0 #mint
[Y1 → RAM 2000-3FFF] as y1 #mint
[Y2 → PPI 4000-5FFF] as y2 #amber
hi -> dec
dec -> y0 : 000
dec -> y1 : 001
dec -> y2 : 010");

problems.prompt: A 4 KB ROM must start at 4000H. What is its address range, and which address lines are decoded?
problems.answer: 4 KB = 2¹² → 12 lines on the chip (A0–A11). Range 4000H–4FFFH; A15–A12 = 0100 must be decoded.

keynotes: Address decoding turns the high address lines into chip-select signals so exactly one chip responds.
Full decoding uses all the high lines (one address per location); partial decoding ignores some, so the chip appears at several addresses.
An 8 KB RAM at 2000H–3FFFH uses A0–A12 on the chip and A15A14A13 = 001 for the select.

sections.title: Memory-mapped I/O versus I/O-mapped I/O
sections.body: Where do you put a keyboard or a display in the address map? There are two answers. In memory-mapped I/O a device lives in the memory address space, so ordinary instructions (MOV, LDA, STA) access it, at the cost of memory addresses. In I/O-mapped (isolated) I/O a separate 256-port space is reached by IN and OUT with the IO/M̅ line high, and the memory map stays free. On the 8085, an I/O-mapped device is accessed with IN and OUT.

questions.prompt: Which instructions access an I/O-mapped device on the 8085?

responses.title: Correct.
responses.body: They assert IO/M̅ so memory does not respond.

keynotes: In memory-mapped I/O a device lives in the memory address space and ordinary instructions (MOV, LDA, STA) access it, at the cost of memory addresses.
In I/O-mapped I/O a separate 256-port space is reached by IN and OUT with the IO/M̅ line high, and the memory map stays free.
On the 8085 an I/O-mapped device is accessed with IN and OUT.

sections.title: Parallel interface: the 8255 PPI
sections.body:
For a beginner’s first real project, the chip you will meet is the 8255 PPI, which gives you three 8-bit ports (A, B, C) programmed through a control word. Mode 0: simple input/output. Mode 1: strobed I/O with handshake. Mode 2: bidirectional. Handshaking means the device signals “data ready”, the processor reads and acknowledges, which is needed when the two run at different speeds.

Build the control word for: port A output, port B input, port C output, Mode 0. D7 = 1 (mode set), D6–D5 = 00, D4 = 0 (A out), D3 = 0 (C upper out), D2 = 0, D1 = 1 (B in), D0 = 0 (C lower out), so 10000010₂ = 82H. Why use handshaking? So no data is lost when the sender and receiver run at different speeds.

worked.why: Program the 8255: port A output, port B input, port C output, Mode 0. Control word: D7 = 1 (mode set), D6–D5 = 00, D4 = 0 (A out), D3 = 0 (C upper out), D2 = 0, D1 = 1 (B in), D0 = 0 (C lower out).

choices.text: So fast and slow devices transfer data without loss.

responses.title: Correct.
responses.body: Each side waits for the other’s signal.

keynotes: The 8255 gives three 8-bit ports (A, B, C) programmed through a control word: Mode 0 simple I/O, Mode 1 strobed I/O with handshake, Mode 2 bidirectional.
Handshaking is needed when the device and processor run at different speeds.
The control word for port A output, port B input, port C output in Mode 0 is 10000010₂ = 82H.

sections.title: Serial interface
sections.body:
Sometimes you only have one wire to spare. Serial transmission sends bits one after another. Asynchronous: each character is framed by a start bit (0) and stop bit(s) (1) so the receiver re-synchronises every byte. Synchronous: a continuous block with a shared clock or sync characters, which is more efficient. RS-232 defines voltage levels and a 9/25-pin connector; USB is the modern serial bus; the 8251 USART does the conversion.

Do the arithmetic. A link at 9600 baud sends 8 data bits, no parity, 1 stop bit (8N1). Bits per character = 1 start + 8 data + 1 stop = 10, so characters per second = 9600/10 = 960. Efficiency = 8/10 = 80%. The start bit exists so the receiver can find the beginning of each character and synchronise its clock.

worked.why: A link at 9600 baud sends 8 data bits, no parity, 1 stop bit (8N1).
Bits per character = 1 start + 8 data + 1 stop = 10, so characters per second = 9600/10.

questions.prompt: What is the purpose of the start bit in asynchronous serial?

choices.text: It marks the beginning of a character so the receiver can synchronise its clock.

responses.title: Correct.
responses.body: The line idles high; the falling edge is the signal.

keynotes: Asynchronous serial frames each character with a start bit (0) and stop bit(s) (1); synchronous sends a continuous block with a shared clock or sync characters.
RS-232 defines voltage levels and a 9/25-pin connector; the 8251 USART does the conversion.
At 9600 baud with 8N1 (10 bits per character) the link moves 960 characters/s, an efficiency of 80%.

sections.title: Interrupts
sections.body:
You can wait for a letter by staring at the letterbox (polling), or the postman can ring your bell (an interrupt). The second leaves the CPU free to do useful work. The 8085 has five hardware interrupts in priority order: TRAP (non-maskable), RST7.5, RST6.5, RST5.5 and INTR. Each RST has a fixed vector (RST7.5 → 003CH, 6.5 → 0034H, 5.5 → 002CH, TRAP → 0024H).

EI/DI enable and disable maskable interrupts; SIM/RIM set and read the masks. The processing steps: finish the instruction, push PC, jump to the vector, run the service routine, RET/EI. The interrupted program continues unaware. The interrupt that cannot be masked is TRAP.

responses.title: Correct.
responses.body: It is non-maskable and highest priority.

figures.caption: Figure 5.1.1 — 8085 interrupt processing
figures.script:
diagram("mode: sequence
[Main program] as p
[8085] as c
[ISR at vector] as i
p -> c : executing
c -> c : interrupt request, EI is on
c -> i : push PC, jump to vector
i -> i : service the device
i --> c : EI, RET
c --> p : resume at the pushed PC");

keynotes: An interrupt lets the device ask for attention so the CPU does useful work meanwhile, unlike polling.
The 8085 has five hardware interrupts in priority order: TRAP (non-maskable), RST7.5, RST6.5, RST5.5 and INTR, with vectors RST7.5 → 003CH, 6.5 → 0034H, 5.5 → 002CH and TRAP → 0024H.
Processing: finish the instruction, push PC, jump to the vector, run the service routine, RET/EI; SIM/RIM set and read the masks.

sections.title: 8086 interrupts and the vector table
sections.body:
The 8086 gives you a whole phone directory of interrupts. It supports 256 interrupt types. Type n has a 4-byte entry (IP then CS) at address 4n in the interrupt vector table, occupying 0000H–03FFH. The sources are hardware (NMI type 2, INTR with type from the PIC), software (INT n) and exceptions (divide error type 0, single-step type 1, breakpoint type 3, overflow type 4). The 8259 PIC prioritises up to 8 (cascaded, 64) devices.

Where is the vector for interrupt type 21H? Address = 4 × 21H = 84H; the four bytes at 0084H–0087H hold IP then CS of the handler. One 8086 interrupt vector occupies four bytes.

worked.why: Where is the vector for interrupt type 21H?
Address = 4 × 21H = 84H; the four bytes at 0084H–0087H hold IP then CS of the handler.

questions.prompt: How many bytes does one 8086 interrupt vector occupy?

problems.prompt: Where in memory is the vector for INT 10H?

keynotes: The 8086 supports 256 interrupt types; type n has a 4-byte entry (IP then CS) at address 4n in the interrupt vector table at 0000H–03FFH.
Sources are hardware (NMI type 2, INTR), software (INT n) and exceptions (divide error 0, single-step 1, breakpoint 3, overflow 4).
The vector for type 21H is at 4 × 21H = 84H, with bytes at 0084H–0087H.

sections.title: Advanced topics: RISC, CISC, control, DSP
sections.body:
Finally, you can look up from the 8085 and 8086 to see where the field is going. Accumulator-based machines (8085) route every result through A; register-based machines (8086 and later) use many registers. Hardwired control is fast; microprogrammed control is flexible. RISC (few simple instructions, pipelined) versus CISC (many complex ones). Multitasking needs protection and memory management support.

And a digital signal processor adds hardware multiply–accumulate and Harvard buses for real-time filtering. So the operation DSPs optimise above all is multiply–accumulate.

questions.prompt: What operation do DSPs optimise above all?

responses.title: Correct.
responses.body: Filters and transforms are sums of products.

problems.prompt: Give one reason a DSP uses a Harvard architecture.
problems.answer: It can fetch an instruction and two data operands in the same cycle, sustaining one multiply–accumulate per cycle for filters.

keynotes: Accumulator-based machines (8085) route every result through A; register-based machines (8086 and later) use many registers.
Hardwired control is fast and microprogrammed control is flexible; RISC has few simple pipelined instructions and CISC many complex ones.
A digital signal processor adds hardware multiply–accumulate and Harvard buses for real-time filtering.
